newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-IRABU PITCHES TWO-HITTER IN FINAL TUNE-UP.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-IRABU PITCHES TWO-HITTER IN FINAL TUNE-UP.

text.p: Japanese right-hander Hideki Irabu turned in a stellar start in his final minor-league appearance before joining the New York Yankees, hurling a two-hitter as Columbus beat Toledo 12-0 on Saturday.

With New York Yankees principal owner George Steinbrenner watching from the owner's box, Irabu went the full seven innings of the first game of the Triple A doubleheader against the Mud Huns, striking out six and walking just one.
The hard-throwing Irabu is scheduled to make his major-league debut for the Yanks in New York's first game following the All-Star break, next Thursday against the Detroit Tigers at Yankee Stadium.
"He is ready," Steinbrenner said afterwards. "That was a darn good second-place Toledo team he shut down. He'll do fine in New York."
Irabu, through an interpretor, said: "I am looking forward to pitching July 10 in New York. This was a final check-up. I have a lot to learn and will keep on learning with the Yankees."
Irabu, who signed a four-year, $12.8 million contract with the Yankees in May after New York obtained his rights in a trade with the San Diego Padres, had three outstanding minor-league starts.
The hefty right-hander was hit hard just once, in a June 25 Double-A contest for the Norwich Navigators against the Binghamton Mets when he allowed five runs and nine hits in five innings.
The walk he issued in Saturday's game was the only free pass the power pitcher allowed in six minor league outings.
Against Toledo, Irabu made 75 pitches, 51 of them strikes, and finished up the final inning for the Clippers by throwing heat clocked in the 95 mph (153 kph) range.
He finished his minor league preparation with an overall 3-1 record, 31 innings pitched, 27 hits, one walk, and 34 strikeouts. He allowed nine runs, eight of them earned.
Billy Connors, assigned by the Yankees to work with Irabu, said his star pupil was ready.
"This was basically spring training in a hurry," said Connors. "Now, it's time to go to New York and show his stuff."
"Today, as opposed to his previous start, he got ahead of the hitters. We worked on holding runners on the bases and he did much better today. The one runner who tried to steal was thrown out."
Irabu was 12-6 with the Chiba Lotte Marines last season and led the Japanese Pacific League with a 2.40 ERA.
Hundreds of added media members are expected to chronicle Irabu's major-league debut in New York.
"I cannot control the media phenomenon," said Irabu. "It is my job to be a baseball player, the rest I cannot control."
Steinbrenner is confident about his prize acquisition.
"This is my project, but I'm betting on Irabu," he said.

Upon joining the Yankees, Irabu will become the fourth Japanese player in the major leagues, joining three other pitchers -- Hideo Nomo of the Los Angeles Dodgers, Shigetoshi Hasegawa of the Anaheim Angels and Takashi Kashiwada of the New York Mets.
